points.en: One error is running without being sent: ambitious, even gifted, but never truly called, treating ministry as a business.
The other error is fleeing when plainly sent (Jonah, Moses), hiding behind unworthiness.
The doctrine of calling delivers from both presumption and disobedient cowardice.
The internal call is a holy compulsion or constraint to preach, more than mere willingness ("woe is me if I do not preach").
The external call is the church's confirmation, after examining the man's gifts and character.
Both must meet: a man does not ordain himself, and an inward fire not confirmed by God's people is only a feeling.
Nearly all the qualifications (1 Timothy 3, Titus 1) are matters of character, such as above reproach, temperate, gentle, not greedy, ruling his house well.
The competence required is modest and ministry-shaped: able to teach, hold sound doctrine, and lead his household.
The world picks leaders by talent and charisma, but God picks shepherds by holiness first.
A new convert is warned against because the danger is pride, being puffed up and falling into the devil's condemnation, not incompetence.
A good reputation with outsiders shows character verified in the marketplace, not just inside the church.
God screens his shepherds by who they are when no one is applauding.
Timothy is told to take heed to himself first and then to the doctrine, so personal life comes before teaching.
A pastor who neglects his own heart is like a fine house on a rotting foundation, and cannot give water from a dry cistern.
Public words should come from a private well refilled daily in secret with God.
The disciplines (prayer, the Word read for his own soul, secret communion with God) are the lifeline that sustains ministry, not optional extras for the very devout.
Without them a pastor can study Scripture professionally and starve spiritually, and the public man becomes a hollow performance.
Image: a baker who never eats the bread; the visible man in the pulpit must be matched by an invisible man on his knees.
Pride is the besetting sin of those who handle holy things because their platform lifts them in others' eyes and makes them a target.
The guard is humility: remembering he is first a sheep who depends on the same grace he proclaims.
Moral failure is a gradual drift through small, excused compromises, not a sudden leap.
The path runs from the unguarded glance to the entertained thought to the secret habit to the public scandal.
No one decides to destroy his life's work; he drifts one unconfessed inch at a time.
Even Paul disciplined himself lest he be disqualified after preaching to others (1 Corinthians 9:27), so no one may presume on his standing.
The man who thinks he needs no guard is in the gravest danger.
Safeguards: accountability to people allowed to ask hard questions, and vigilant guard over the eyes, schedule and private hours.
Safeguards: refusing to minister in isolation, and confessing sin immediately while it is small.
The aim is to finish well and keep the faith to the end, not merely to begin well.
Guarding his marriage is part of this vigilance (2 Timothy 4:7).
